# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 17 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 17

---

1 For great are your judgments and hard to describe; therefore undisciplined souls went astray.

2 For when lawless men supposed that they held the holy nation in their power, prisoners themselves, they lay bound with chains of darkness and long night, shut up beneath their roofs, banished from eternal providence.

3 For while they thought to remain hidden in their secret sins, they were scattered beneath a dark curtain of forgetfulness, terribly frightened and troubled by apparitions.

4 For not even the inner room that contained them kept them from fear; but sounds full of dread rang around them, and grim phantoms with sullen faces appeared to them.

5 And no force of fire was strong enough to give light, nor were the brilliant flames of the stars able to illuminate that dreadful night.

6 Nothing shone through to them but an eerie fire that ignited itself, full of terror; and in their fright they considered what they saw worse than the vision they could not see.

7 The tricks of their magic art were exposed as worthless, and their boasted wisdom was put to shame.

8 For those who promised to drive away fears and disorders from sick souls were themselves sick with a ridiculous terror.

9 For even if nothing alarming actually threatened them, they were unnerved by the passing of reptiles and the hissing of serpents,

10 and they perished trembling, refusing to look even at the air — which they could not escape no matter which way they turned.

11 For wickedness is cowardly, condemned by its own inner witness; and pressed hard by conscience, it always imagines the worst.

12 For fear is nothing but the abdication of the help that comes from reason;

13 and the inner expectation, being deficient, counts its ignorance as more than the cause of the torment.

14 But they throughout that night — powerless as it was, coming upon them from the recesses of powerless Hades — sleeping the same sleep,

15 were now driven by monstrous apparitions, now paralyzed by the collapse of their own souls; for sudden and unexpected terror came upon them.

16 Then if anyone fell down, he was kept under guard, shut up in a prison not made of iron;

17 for whether he was a farmer or a shepherd or a laborer at work in the countryside, he was overtaken and endured the inescapable doom; for they were all bound with a single chain of darkness.

18 Whether it was a whistling wind, or a melodious sound of birds among the spreading branches, or the rhythmic sound of rushing water,

19 or the crashing din of rocks hurled down, or the unseen galloping of leaping animals, or the roaring of fierce wild beasts, or an echo resounding from a hollow mountain — these things paralyzed them with terror.

20 For the whole world was bathed in brilliant light and went about its work unimpeded;

21 while over those people alone there was spread a heavy night — an image of the darkness destined to receive them; but they were more burdensome to themselves than the darkness was.

---

**Council Notes:**

Chapter 17 is the most sustained piece of psychological description in the Apocrypha. The author turns the plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21–23) into an exploration of terror, guilt, and irrational fear. The chapter has notably difficult Greek in vv. 13–15, where the syntax is compressed and the meaning debated.

V. 2: "banished from eternal providence" — LOGOS's "banished" preferred over EMET's "exiles from." The Egyptians' darkness is framed as exile from divine light — a theological point.

V. 4: "grim phantoms with sullen faces" — all three largely agree. PNEUMA's "gloomy shapes with sullen, scowling faces" adds "scowling" not in the Greek; trimmed.

V. 6: "an eerie fire that ignited itself" — PNEUMA's rendering captures the sense well. Greek αὐτόματος = spontaneous. LOGOS's "eerie fire that ignited itself" adopted.

V. 11: "condemned by its own inner witness" — a powerful moral-psychological observation. LOGOS "condemned by its own witness," PNEUMA "condemns itself with its own inner voice." SOPHIA: "condemned by its own inner witness."

Vv. 12–13: These verses are notoriously difficult. EMET maintains literalness to the Greek structure; LOGOS clarifies the argument; PNEUMA paraphrases extensively. LOGOS structure adopted with EMET's wording where possible.

V. 14: "powerless Hades" — the darkness is called an emanation of Hades (death), itself described as "powerless" — because God holds ultimate authority over it (cf. 16:13). All three agents note this theological point.

V. 21: "an image of the darkness destined to receive them" — the darkness is proleptically the darkness of death/Sheol that awaits the wicked. LOGOS's "foretaste" (PNEUMA) is evocative but adds to the text; "image" retained with "destined to receive them."
